subject: Is the US or Europe better off?
body: Plus: the Democrats are not in great shape ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser IS THE US OR EUROPE BETTER OFF? Srinidhi Balakrishnan Commissioning Editor, FT Opinion ‌ ‌ July 15 2026 The general view, writes Martin Wolf, is that when compared to the US, the contemporary European economy is a dying duck. But is this really a fair analysis? We should remember those bold words of “life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness” in the Declaration of Independence, says Martin. Indeed, when we look at life expectancy or homicide rates, the US appears far from superior to its peers across the Atlantic. Economically, however, America remains stronger. Here, Martin notes an interesting caveat: while the US has grown faster than Europe, it has not necessarily wound up relatively richer than at the start. Elsewhere, Edward Luce considers the splintering of the Democratic Party. The Democrats are split between a radicalised younger vote, “increasingly Maga-like in tactics and tone”, and an ageing establishment short of ideas. “The portents for the 2028 presidential primaries are not all good”, writes Edward. Constanze Stelzenmüller, director of the Center on the US and Europe at the Brookings Institution, argues we are not on course for a Nato divorce — yet. The recent Ankara summit went a lot better than feared. But the fact remains: Europe needs to work around vacillating US support. “Europeans need to plan for two distinct scenarios: a ‘fight tonight’ contingency, or a larger-scale military aggression in a few years.” And Anjana Ahuja writes that the rather bland-sounding Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance might well prove to be the final nail in the coffin for US science. WHAT YOU’VE BEEN SAYING ‌ ‌ Strong carbon pricing underpins Europe’s competitiveness — Letter from Eliot Whittington, Director, Corporate Leaders Groups, University of Cambridge Institute for Sustainability Leadership, Cambridge, UK in response to a report: Lakshmi Mittal claims “Europe’s emissions trading system is not working for industry”, and sets out his shopping list of requested support, as the price of climate action. But in challenging the current carbon trading system he is not speaking for the whole of his industry, let alone the whole of energy-intense manufacturing, clean tech or wider industrial, service and financial sectors. Many businesses we work with . . . are counting on a clear carbon price signal to keep underpinning the business case for investments in new solutions. subject: Ukraine to buy Chinese drone parts with EU funds
body: Plus, Trump’s return to war with Iran and BYD signals wider European expansion ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Irwin Cruz Digital Editor ‌ ‌ July 15 2026 Good morning and welcome to FirstFT. In today’s newsletter: * Ukraine cleared to buy Chinese drone parts with EU funds * Donald Trump’s return to war with Iran offers no clear path to victory * BYD executive signals intensified European expansion * Ed Miliband trails Shabana Mahmood in race to become Burnham’s chancellor You can listen to today’s top news stories in the FT News Briefing podcast. ‌ We begin with Ukraine, which will be allowed to spend funds from an EU defence loan on Chinese drone components. What we know: Kyiv has obtained a carve-out for part of a €6bn tranche to purchase drone components from China, according to two people familiar with the decision. The funds mark the first allocation from a wider Ukraine support loan, under which €60bn is earmarked for defence procurement. Why it matters: The decision highlights the gaps that remain in the EU’s domestic defence production, despite a push to strengthen Europe’s industrial base by tying aid for Ukraine to procurement in the continent. The carve-out also makes stark China’s role in supplying both sides in the more than four-year conflict. While the EU has accused Beijing of being “the key enabler of Russia’s war” against Ukraine as a major supplier to Moscow’s military-industrial complex, it acknowledges that Kyiv’s arms industry also relies on Chinese components. Read the exclusive story from Paola Tamma and Henry Foy. Here’s what else I’m keeping tabs on today: * Economic data: The US Federal Reserve publishes its latest Beige Book on economic conditions. * US: Attorney-general nominee Todd Blanche appears before the Senate judiciary committee at the start of a two-day confirmation hearing. * Results: ASML, BlackRock, BNY, Handelsbanken and Morgan Stanley report earnings. FIVE MORE TOP STORIES 1. This week Donald Trump seemed to relish the return to battering Iran with near-daily strikes, touting the US military “knocking the hell” out of the country. However, it remains unclear how the US president will limit the costs of the latest escalation, particularly as the midterm elections loom. 2. Exclusive: BYD can unseat Toyota as the world’s biggest carmaker by sales without access to the US market, according to the executive spearheading the Chinese group’s global ambitions, suggesting it will intensify an aggressive European expansion. 3. Daniel Ek’s body-scanning start-up Neko Health has raised $700mn in a founding round from investors that included Mark Zuckerberg, Ari Emanuel and Maria Sharapova, valuing the eight-year-old Swedish company at almost $7bn. 4. Exclusive: Oracle is winning the race to sell top-secret cloud services to Japan that the US says are critical to secure intelligence sharing between Tokyo and allies as they face growing threats from China. The Texas-based company is leading Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Google to provide the “air-gapped” cloud. 5. Ed Miliband’s opponents in the Labour Party believe he has failed in his bid to become UK chancellor, with home secretary Shabana Mahmood now seen by some MPs as favourite to take the role in Andy Burnham’s government. * Who is Anneliese Midgley? The Knowsley MP and former Britpop stalwart has been credited as a key influence on the incoming UK prime minister Andy Burnham. THE BIG READ © FT montage/Kyodo/Getty Images Yttrium, discovered in Sweden in the late 18th century, has huge strategic value in the production of the computer chips that are the backbone of AI. It is also one of the niche metals at the centre of a raging geopolitical storm. The vast majority of yttrium, along with many other minerals used in global manufacturing processes, is produced in China. But as its tit-for-tat trade war with the US escalates, Beijing has increasingly restricted access to its supplies of critical metals. Even before Beijing’s introduction of export controls, experts were warning that ageing mines and soaring demand for the metals might mean shortages. Now, western countries are feeling the effects of losing a metals-processing industry they allowed to move to China. Camilla Hodgson writes on the new era of resource nationalism. WE’RE ALSO READING . . . * Helsing’s ‘crazy’ valuation: The German drone start-up’s fundraise gave it a higher revenue multiple than many of its peers, raising concerns of a defence tech bubble. * Rich list obsession: Wealth rankings have caught the attention of everyone from tax authorities to activists, but how reliable are they? * Chinese economy: The country has reported GDP growth of 4.3 per cent in the second quarter, the lowest in more than three years. CHART OF THE DAY Is the US or Europe better off? If one compares the US with the Eurozone on growth since 2000, its performance is hugely superior. But if one compares relative GDP per head, this is not true: Eurozone GDP per head has risen relative to the US’s, writes Martin Wolf. TAKE A BREAK FROM THE NEWS . . . Jude Bellingham has been one of the standout players at the Fifa men’s World Cup. If the England midfielder can repeat his match-winning feats in today’s semi-final against Argentina, it will put “brand Bellingham” on track to become one of the most valuable in the world’s biggest sport, writes Samuel Agini. subject: Before you build that tool, ask this first
body: Hi Umair! How’s it going?? 😊 So we've been doing a lot of internal tool building at Lonely Octopus lately. And it's been genuinely exciting. But it's also taught me something important that I think a lot of people skip when they start getting comfortable building with AI. Just because you can build something doesn't mean you should. Here's the question I now ask before we start building anything: Do we actually need a custom tool here, or does a solution already exist? It sounds obvious. But when building becomes fast and fun, and with AI it really does, there's a real temptation to just start making things. You hit a problem in your workflow. You immediately think "I could build something for this." And before you know it, you've spent a week on a tool that solves a problem a $15/month subscription already handles better. I've done this. More than once. So now our first step is always: go look for the existing solution first. Search for the tool, try the free tier, see if it does the job. Only if the answer is "no" or the price doesn't make sense for what we need, then we start building. About half the time, something already exists. The other half? That's when building gets really interesting. Because you're building something that genuinely can't be bought. Something custom to exactly how your team works. That's the right reason to build. Not because it's fun. Not because you can. But because nothing out there actually solves your specific problem. Something worth keeping in mind the next time you feel the urge to build. subject: Wall Street’s ‘off the charts’ quarter
body: Plus, IBM shares plunge and DeepSeek weighs new fundraising ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Benjamin Wilhelm Newsletter Editor ‌ ‌ July 15 2026 Good morning and welcome to FirstFT. In today’s newsletter: * Wall Street banks shatter records on AI-stock trading frenzy * IBM shares plunge 25 per cent * China’s air pollution clean-up loses momentum ‌ We begin on Wall Street, where four of the world’s biggest banks unveiled record quarterly profits as they cash in on a speculative trading frenzy in AI-linked groups. Almost ‘as good as it gets’: JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Bank of America yesterday reported combined equities trading revenues of $19.3bn — far in excess of what analysts had been expecting and 72 per cent higher than a year ago. Across their wider businesses, the banks posted a combined $42.7bn in net income. The results underscore how the rush to build AI infrastructure is driving a boom in Wall Street earnings, with soaring stock prices in the US, China, Korea and Taiwan and sharp moves in equity markets that have boosted the banks’ trading arms. Executives described a Goldilocks environment for equities trading with big initial public offerings such as SpaceX, elevated activity in Asia and significant changes to the make-up of indices. “It’s getting close to as good as it gets. We just don’t know how long it’s going to last,” JPMorgan chief executive Jamie Dimon said. AI-stock trading boom: Banks have shifted their trading businesses away from taking directional bets in recent years, and they now focus primarily on facilitating and financing trades for hedge funds and other specialist trading firms. Market volatility, particularly around the semiconductor stocks and hyperscalers riding a wave of enthusiasm for AI, has helped stock traders to a string of record-high performances. Still, the second quarter was “off the charts”, analysts at Oppenheimer said. Read the full story. Here’s what else I’m keeping tabs on today: * Chinese economy: China publishes second-quarter GDP data, as well as the house price index, retail sales figures and industrial output for June. Here are five things to watch in today’s data release. * Trade: The UK-India free trade agreement comes into force. WAS THIS FORWARDED TO YOU? If you’re an FT subscriber, sign up here to get this newsletter delivered straight to your inbox. If you’re new to the FT, take out a subscription here. Sent every weekday. FIVE MORE TOP STORIES 1. IBM issued a profit warning that sent its shares plunging, as customers raced to redirect spending to servers and storage ahead of price increases driven by the AI boom. Shares closed 25 per cent lower, in the biggest drop since at least 1972 and exceeding the fall it recorded during the 1987 Black Monday crash. * More tech news: DeepSeek is considering raising new funds just one month after closing its first round, as China’s leading AI lab seeks to accelerate expansion of its infrastructure. * Nvidia’s China chip crackdown: The $5.1tn chipmaker has intensified due diligence in Singapore, Malaysia and Japan, reflecting Washington’s push to prevent its products from reaching China. 2. Donald Trump has said he will drop his demand for a 20 per cent fee on cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz, as the US and Iran fight for control of the critical waterway. The US president said on his Truth Social platform yesterday that instead of a fee, which he had expected Gulf allies to pay, the countries would instead invest in the US. * Related news: Washington and Tehran are in their most dangerous period of fighting since a fragile April truce, as the US seeks to stop Iran from asserting control over the Strait of Hormuz. 3. New Zealand’s prime minister has warned against a return to the “sugar rush economics” under Jacinda Ardern-era Labour, saying the economy would be plunged into higher levels of debt, inflation and unemployment. Christopher Luxon told the FT that elections in November would test voters’ resolve to stick with his centre-right National Party government’s economic repair plan. Read the full interview. 4. China’s monthly car exports rose to a record 1mn cars in June as part of an overall surge in trade that will heighten tensions with partners such as the EU. Electric vehicle exports surged but also sales of electric railway locomotives, electric motorcycles and bicycles as China leads the move away from fossil-fuel-powered vehicles into the era of electrification. 5. Warren Buffett excluded the Gates Foundation from his annual donation of shares, directing nearly $6bn of stock to four family-linked charities. The omission of the charity yesterday follows revelations about Bill Gates’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein. RIP THE US STATE DEPARTMENT © White House/News Pictures/Shutterstock As the official face and sometimes swaggering enforcer of America’s position in the world, the US state department is accustomed to extraordinary respect abroad. Since the end of the cold war, the country’s ambassadors and envoys have often dominated their hosts with the authority of imperial satraps. But 18 months into Trump’s second term, the department is not just sidelined; it appears under siege. WE’RE ALSO READING . . . * Democratic Party infighting: A fractious opposition is doing everything it can to spurn an open goal, writes Edward Luce. * ‘Unprecedented’ drone assault: Ukraine said it has hit more than 110 Russian vessels in nine days in the Sea of Azov. * The new Mechanical Turk: AI’s evolution offers fresh opportunities for hoodwinkers and charlatans, writes Sarah O’Connor. CHART OF THE DAY China’s effort to clean up its air pollution is losing momentum amid rising coal production and unfavourable weather conditions. FT analysis of the data since 2000 shows both the extent of the country’s progress and its latest battle to keep a lid on pollution. The vast nation dramatically reduced harmful fine particulate matter, with levels falling almost 60 per cent from the 2013 peak by the end of last year. This led to a 30 per cent fall in the share of hospital admissions caused by this pollution. TAKE A BREAK FROM THE NEWS . . . Sony’s recent announcement that it will discontinue the production of physical PlayStation game discs from 2028 has prompted a furious response from players. The industry’s pivot towards a digital-only future signals a waning regard for fans and the preservation of cultural memory, writes Tom Faber. subject: when life hits you in the face
body: Hey Umair, So last weekend, during muay thai sparring, this guy hit me in the face.. And you know what, I hit that m#@$@%^ker back! A lesson I've learned training combat sports is that everything is not going to go your way. I can train with my coach, hit pads and punching bags all I want… But when it comes time to fight someone for a full 3 minutes, you have to accept you might get hit in the face a few times. And when you do, instead of taking it the wrong way… You gotta reflect and learn what you could have done differently to prevent it. In so many ways, running a business is very similar. You'll start all excited with your business idea… But when you start reaching out to people, nobody responds.. When you make that first YouTube video, you might spend a whole week on it only to get 10 views from your friends and family. And that's how life goes. It humbles you to help you learn where you need to improve. -Patrick Work with Me ↓ P.S. subject: Both World Cup semifinals are clashes of giants – one is the much hotter ticket
body:
The 2026 World Cup semifinals feature four giants of international soccer and around $5billion worth of playing talent. They pit the world’s top-ranked team, France, against No. 3 Spain; and No. 2 Argentina against No. 4 England. Each matchup boasts megastars, such as Kylian Mbappé, Lionel Messi, Lamine Yamal and Harry Kane; and looks, at first glance, like a red-hot ticket.

But in reality, one is much hotter than the other.

As of Sunday night, tickets to the second semifinal, England against Argentina, on Wednesday are selling for around twice as much as tickets to the first semifinal, France vs Spain, a day earlier.

subject: Trump’s plan for Europe is falling apart
body: Plus: the era of machines pretending to be humans has begun ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser TRUMP’S PLAN FOR EUROPE IS FALLING APART Ursula Milton Commissioning Editor, FT Opinion ‌ ‌ July 14 2026 Europe clearly matters to America, writes Gideon Rachman. The Trump administration’s National Security Strategy asserts the continent is “strategically and culturally vital to the United States”. But European parties and politicians the administration regard as “patriotic” are losing power, as Viktor Orbán did in Hungary, or distancing themselves from the US president. The problem, Gideon notes, is that Trump’s experience at home has taught him he can insult and demean opponents and they will come crawling back. But in Europe, this type of behaviour has provoked strong reactions and the US President has managed to alienate potential allies in Italy, Germany, France and the UK. Elsewhere, Sarah O’Connor looks at the role humans have played in training — and sometimes mimicking — technology. She highlights the nascent “synthetic sampling” industry, where LLMs role-play as humans and then answer surveys based on their “opinions”. The era of humans pretending to be machines is over, she concludes. The era of machines pretending to be humans has begun. Scientist and UCLA professor Prineha Narang urges the US to prioritise creating a market and securing the supply chain for quantum computing. A guaranteed buyer at a national laboratory will do for the industry what early defence and space contracts did for silicon, she argues. Those models were the mainstay of motoring stability in those very positive years for both British and European motor manufacturers. body: Plus, Nvidia halves Asia buyer list and Rothschild’s UK investment bank ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Irwin Cruz Digital Editor ‌ ‌ July 14 2026 Good morning and welcome to FirstFT. In today’s newsletter: * US launches strikes as Iran targets tankers with missiles * Nvidia halves Asia buyer list in China chip crackdown * Profits drop at Rothschild’s UK investment banking arm * How Donald Trump sidelined America’s diplomats You can listen to today’s top news stories in the FT News Briefing podcast. ‌ We begin in the Middle East, where the US struck Iran again on Monday as the Islamic republic targeted two tankers with cruise missiles in the Strait of Hormuz. The latest: American forces undertook the sixth wave of attacks since President Donald Trump last week resumed US air strikes in retaliation for Iran hitting commercial ships navigating the strait and declared that a ceasefire intended to open the waterway was “over”. US Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, said Monday’s strikes were intended to “continue imposing a heavy cost on Iranian forces and degrade their ability to attack innocent civilians and commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz”. Earlier, Trump posted on Truth Social that the waterway, through which a fifth of global oil shipments typically pass, was “OPEN” and told Fox News the US would be “taking over the strait” and become its “guardian”. However, late on Monday the United Arab Emirates’ defence ministry said two tankers — the Mombasa and the Bahia — “were targeted by two Iranian cruise missiles in the southern passage of the Strait of Hormuz in Omani territorial waters”, killing one crew member and injuring eight others. Market reaction: The military clashes raise the risk of a return to full-blown conflict between Washington and Tehran, and have driven up oil prices over recent days. Brent crude, the international benchmark, was 1.9 per cent higher in early Asia trading at $84.90 a barrel. It settled 10 per cent higher on Monday, the highest level since June 12, as tensions flared between Washington and Tehran. * Related news: DP World is planning to build a new port on the UAE’s east coast that would reduce Dubai’s dependence on its flagship Jebel Ali hub and bypass the Strait of Hormuz. * Mobile surveillance: Middle Eastern mobile networks were repeatedly hit with cyber attacks to track the locations of US personnel and contractors during the Iran war. And here’s what else I’m keeping tabs on today: * Economic data: The US releases June inflation data. * France: The country marks Bastille Day. * UK: Chancellor Rachel Reeves and Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey deliver their annual Mansion House speeches. The government’s financial services AI adoption plan will be officially launched at the event. * US: Kevin Warsh presents the semi-annual monetary policy report to the House committee on financial services for the first time as Federal Reserve chair. * Results: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup and Wells Fargo report second-quarter earnings. FIVE MORE TOP STORIES 1. Exclusive: Nvidia has more than halved the number of Asian customers authorised to buy its AI chips after creating a new “white list” of companies that have passed tougher compliance checks aimed at preventing the products from reaching China. 2. Exclusive: Rothschild’s UK investment bank paid out higher bonuses last year, eating into deal fees and dragging profits lower. The results highlight how the long-awaited recovery in mergers and acquisitions has begun to lift revenues for investment banks, while also pushing up pay as firms compete to reward dealmakers. 3. Britons flying to Gibraltar from the UK will have to go through the EU’s contentious new electronic border system from this week. The rocky outpost will become a de facto part of the bloc’s Schengen free-movement area after midnight tonight, when a new UK-EU treaty comes into force. 4. US small-cap stocks are bucking years of underperformance to enjoy their best returns in more than 20 years, as investors start to look beyond high-flying big tech companies to lowly valued stocks benefiting from the AI investment boom. 5. China’s monthly car exports rose 71.2 per cent from a year earlier to 1.06mn, putting the country on track to export more than 10mn cars this year. The new record comes as part of an overall surge in trade that will heighten tensions with partners such as the EU. THE BIG READ © White House/News Pictures/Shutterstock As the official face and sometimes swaggering enforcer of America’s position in the world, the US state department is accustomed to extraordinary respect abroad. Since the end of the cold war, the country’s ambassadors and envoys have often dominated their hosts with the authority of imperial satraps. But 18 months into Trump’s second term, the department is not just sidelined; it appears under siege. Abandoning the precedent of the past 60 years, the US president has brushed aside the foreign service officers who have typically run at least two-thirds of embassies. Of the 101 nominations for ambassadorships in his second term, just nine were career diplomats. All this is against the backdrop of swingeing cuts to the department, whose workforce has shrunk by more than 3,000, over 20 per cent, since Trump resumed office. Administration officials present the shake-up as an overdue reform of a bureaucratic arm of government. Insiders warn of a crude politicisation and a purge of experts. What does this mean for US diplomacy and America abroad? WE’RE ALSO READING . . . * Something to mimic: The Trump investment accounts may have shortcomings but these cannot fundamentally undermine what is a good plan, writes Patrick Jenkins. * UK immigration: Andy Burnham, who is set to take over as prime minister next week, is looking to succeed where Sir Keir Starmer failed. * The new Mechanical Turk: AI’s evolution offers fresh opportunities for hoodwinkers and charlatans, writes Sarah O’Connor. CHART OF THE DAY Xavier Niel and Sunil Mittal have placed big bets on Vodafone and BT. One reason the billionaires piled on to the UK telecoms operators is their depressed share prices. The London-listed groups have underperformed European peers, including Deutsche Telekom, Orange and Telecom Italia, over the past decade. TAKE A BREAK FROM THE NEWS . . . Meta enlisted uber-influencer Kylie Jenner to bring its smart glasses to a broader demographic. But instead of creating buzz, the partnership generated backlash, with critics calling the move “surveillance chic”. subject: Invitation to connect with Apple
body: Hi Umair, We recently invited you to talk with us about opportunities at Apple, but we haven't yet heard back from you. If you're still interested, here are the details. Event Details Apple Retail - Singapore - Phone Screening 13-Jul-2026 - 17-Jul-2026 Venue Details This will be an On-Phone Event. We’ll contact you using the phone number provided in your profile. RSVP now Before you RSVP, we need you to take care of a few things: 1. Create or update your job profile. Log in to your profile on Jobs at Apple and ensure your contact information is up to date. The primary email address on your profile should match the email address on this invitation. If you don’t have a job profile, this is your opportunity to create one. 2. Learn about Apple Retail. While you’re on Jobs at Apple, learn more about why people come to work at Apple. Read about our various roles and watch videos with real store employees — this is a great way to prepare for your phone appointment. 3. Register. Register for a convenient time to speak on the phone with a member of Apple’s hiring team. If you have any questions about registration or if the event is showing full, please reply back so we can provide assistance. RSVP now. 4. Joining the event. For virtual events, please start your webex link no earlier than 5 minutes before your scheduled session and plan to be with us for the entire duration. The link will be in your registration confirmation email or you can log on to your RSVP.apple.com to view the details. For on-site events, please arrive 15 minutes early on your reserved date and time, and plan to be with us for the entire duration. For on-phone events, we’ll contact you using the phone number provided. Feel free to dress business casual. This invitation will remain open for a limited time, so reserve your place before it’s too late. Registration deadline: 16-Jul-2026. If you’re unavailable for any of the times provided, please reply to this email. If you’re no longer interested in pursuing opportunities at Apple, please opt out to avoid receiving any further notifications about this event. Apple is committed to working with and providing reasonable accommodations to job applicants with physical or mental disabilities. Should you need any accommodations to participate in the hiring event, or if you have any other questions or concerns about the event, please reply to this email. We look forward to speaking with you soon. Regards, Apple www.apple.com/jobs/sg If you prefer not to receive emails from Apple regarding this event please click here Apple is an equal opportunity employer that is committed to inclusion and diversity. subject: Investors fret over Asian chipmakers
body: Plus, companies turn to Chinese AI models to cut costs and Jane Fraser’s ruthless remake of Citigroup ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Benjamin Wilhelm Newsletter Editor ‌ ‌ July 14 2026 Good morning and welcome to FirstFT. In today’s newsletter: * Why investors are alarmed about Asian chipmakers * Companies turn to Chinese AI models to cut costs * Why China still believes in the power of rote memorisation ‌ We begin with investor anxiety over Asia’s chipmakers and their stranglehold on emerging-market indices. What to know: Investors are cutting back bets on Asia’s chipmakers, as a $1.8tn rally that propelled them into the ranks of the world’s biggest companies starts to unwind amid anxiety about their dominance of emerging-market indices. Fidelity International and BlackRock are among fund firms harbouring concerns over the sustainability of a bull run in stocks such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp, South Korea’s SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, which are crucial suppliers in the race among US hyperscalers for AI chips and data centres. The trio has together nearly doubled in market value over the past six months and now accounts for about 29 per cent of the broad MSCI Emerging Markets index, more than most individual countries, despite a recent sell-off in SK Hynix and Samsung. Chipmaker dominance: The three stocks, which all have a market capitalisation of about $1tn or more, have dominated gains in emerging markets so far in 2026, as shortages push up chip prices. Their weighting in the MSCI EM index, which is tracked by many developing market investors, is now nearly triple that of all its Indian stocks, with SK Hynix’s weighting alone larger than Brazil and South Africa combined. What investors are saying: The index concentration, plus the proliferation of leveraged bets on Korea’s chipmakers that magnify share price moves, were “markers in the sand”, said Caroline Shaw, multi-asset portfolio manager at Fidelity International. These are “the type of thing we look for to say: is this overdone?” While she declined to comment on individual stocks, she said she had reduced exposure to growth stocks and was instead looking at “more unloved companies” in emerging markets. Here’s what else we know. And here’s what else I’m keeping tabs on today: * Economic data: China publishes June trade figures, Singapore releases advance second-quarter GDP estimates and the US reports June inflation data. * Wall Street: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup and Wells Fargo report second-quarter results. FIVE MORE TOP STORIES 1. The US military has launched its sixth round of strikes against Iran in less than a week, extending its military escalation after Donald Trump said Washington would hit Iran “hard” on Monday and Tuesday nights. Brent crude, the international benchmark, settled nearly 10 per cent higher on Monday at $83.30 a barrel, the highest level since June 12. Read the full story. * Related news: DP World is planning to build a new port on the UAE’s east coast that would reduce Dubai’s dependence on its flagship Jebel Ali hub and bypass the Strait of Hormuz. * Markets: US stocks and Treasuries dropped yesterday after an escalation in tensions between Washington and Tehran triggered fresh bets on higher inflation and interest rates. 2. Companies from Silicon Valley to Europe are turning to Chinese AI models as they try to cut the cost of using the technology and reduce reliance on US frontier labs. DoorDash, Siemens and Airbnb are among the groups that have adopted AI tools built in China such as DeepSeek and Z.ai. 3. Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service had “no viable basis in law or fact” and was brought for the “improper purpose” of legitimising a legally dubious deal, a US judge ruled on Monday. The withering 56-page decision casts doubt on whether the president and his family will be able to reap the benefits of a settlement that granted immunity from existing IRS tax audits. 4. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has called on JPMorgan Chase boss Jamie Dimon to say whether he lobbied the UK government against a tax on bankers’ bonuses on the advice of child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Here are more details. 5. US states including California and New York have filed an antitrust lawsuit to block Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, threatening a costly delay to a $110bn deal that the Trump administration has backed. The states assert the deal would weaken competition from the licensing of basic cable channels to blockbuster movie releases. JANE FRASER’S RUTHLESS REMAKE OF CITIGROUP © FT montage/Bloomberg Jane Fraser has reinvented Citigroup. When she took over in 2021 the bank was bloated, overly complex and still reeling from the embarrassing $900mn payment it mistakenly made to creditors instead of a $7.8mn interest payment. Results out tomorrow will demonstrate progress, but industry analysts and executives say Fraser now needs to prove she can turn a leaner Citi into a faster-growing one. WE’RE ALSO READING . . . * China’s decline: The country’s vaunted AI prowess is concealing deep rot elsewhere in its economy, writes Ruchir Sharma. * India’s education system: Huge disparities and brutally competitive exams mean only a select few secure good degrees and well-paid jobs. * Asia’s capital surplus: Investors have favoured Japan and South Korea over larger domestic-focused economies, writes Trinh Nguyen. CHART OF THE DAY Europe and the US would need to invest an extra $23.6tn over the next 25 years to end their reliance on China in critical industries such as manufacturing and technology, an economic analysis suggests. TAKE A BREAK FROM THE NEWS . . . Throughout decades of political, economic and technological transformation in China, the art of learning ancient texts by heart has persisted. Shanghai correspondent Thomas Hale explains why the country still believes in the power of rote memorisation. Yueyang Tower in the southern province of Hunan. body: EU ups ante, tech stocks tumble, bank bonanza ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Darren Dodd Writer and Commissioning Editor ‌ ‌ July 13 2026 TODAY’S TOP NEWS STORIES * Donald Trump said the US would reinstate its naval blockade of Iran and charge a 20 per cent fee on cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz, as Washington and Tehran battle for control of the critical waterway. * Dubai is planning a new port to bypass the strait, the FT revealed, marking a seismic change for the emirate as a global trade hub. * UK counterterror police have taken over the investigation into the murder of former Conservative government minister Ann Widdecombe after “new information and evidence” came to light over the killing of the 78-year-old. ‌ Good evening. Brussels is moving towards a ban on children using social media in the latest attempt by authorities to rein in the powers of Big Tech. European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen has floated “phased and gradual access for different age ranges”, arguing that tech companies are not doing enough to protect children from the negative effects of being online. Several countries, including France, have grown impatient and have imposed their own restrictions. Social media companies argue they already have a number of protections in place for children, such as Instagram’s Teen Accounts, which have screen-time limits and extra privacy settings to avoid contact from strangers. The EU is also set to give itself new powers to fine the companies for failing to protect consumers — and especially children — from online spending traps. In addition, the EU warned Meta last week over the addictive nature of feeds on Instagram and Facebook. In the US, Meta has already been held liable in a landmark legal case that found its platforms are designed to be addictive to children. The EU has several other investigations into the platforms under its watershed Digital Services Act, which polices content online, but action is spreading internationally, too. Last month, the UK announced a ban on under-16s using social media platforms including Snapchat, YouTube and TikTok, insisting that it would “make our children happier” and “change the conversations” that parents have with their children. The UK move builds on Australia’s pioneering ban on kids using the platforms. Meta is also in hot water in India after a BBC investigation uncovered evidence that Instagram was showing advertisements and content promoting child sexual exploitation and abuse material to users. The investigation alleged that some of these ads directed users to Telegram channels where the content was available for purchase, although Meta disputes the suggestion that it “knowingly and deliberately” targeted users. The Indian government has issued a separate notice over WhatsApp’s planned new feature, which would display usernames instead of phone numbers, on concerns that it opens the door to large-scale impersonation and fraud. As revealed by the FT last month, Meta meanwhile is racing to replace human moderation with generative AI across its platforms as it undergoes a broader cost-cutting drive. The switch to using large language models to review content and advertising could help the $1.4tn company save billions of dollars a year. ‌ PICTURE OF THE DAY A house is engulfed in flames in a village near Moscow after a second consecutive day of Ukrainian drone attacks as Kyiv stepped up its long-range strike campaign against Russia © via Reuters ‌ ECONOMICS * Europe imported record volumes of liquefied natural gas from Russia’s leading LNG project in the first half of 2026, months before an EU ban on Russian gas imports comes into effect. * Europe and the US would need to invest an extra $23.6tn over the next 25 years to end their reliance on China in critical industries, a study suggests. * The UK could hold an expanded Budget this autumn under Andy Burnham, who is set to become prime minister on July 20. Chancellor Rachel Reeves has made a last-minute pitch to stay on as a senior minister under Burnham. * The UK could benefit from a £33bn economic boost if it accelerates plans to digitise its financial markets, according to the chair of a new task force. ‌ MARKETS * Tech stocks fell and oil prices jumped as events in the Middle East reverberated across markets, hitting Asian chipmakers hard. * Chinese regulators are pressuring rating agencies to cut back on triple-A designations for higher-interest borrowers amid creditworthiness concerns. ‌ NUMBER OF THE DAY 27 PER CENT The increase in fees expected to be announced by the five largest US banks — JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America and Citigroup — when they report second-quarter earnings this week. ‌ BUSINESS * US states including California and New York have filed an antitrust lawsuit to block Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery. * Intel will invest €5bn to expand semiconductor manufacturing in Ireland, in a boost for Europe’s ambitions to build a stronger chip industry. * Companies from Silicon Valley to Europe are turning to Chinese AI models as they try to cut costs and reduce their dependence on US frontier labs. * An employer push to make staff use AI more has backfired, as costs start to hit home. * JPMorgan boss Jamie Dimon was pressed over whether he lobbied the UK against a bankers’ bonus tax on the advice of child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. * Volkswagen’s chief confirmed a plan to axe 50,000 jobs, underlining his determination to cut costs despite opposition from VW’s supervisory board. * Freshfields has forced out partners after a pay overhaul at the UK-based “magic circle” law firm in an effort to drive growth, the FT revealed. ‌ TRADE * The UK and Switzerland are loosening visa restrictions as part of a services trade deal, enabling professionals to work in each other’s countries visa-free for 90 days a year. ‌ SOME GOOD NEWS ‌ ‌ Deep-ocean vent systems represent natural laboratories for studying life in extreme conditions. New research shows how this extreme world could help drive important innovations in biotechnology, including discovering new antimicrobial molecules for fighting disease, diagnostic tools to track the spread of pathogens, and even new ways to tackle plastic pollution. © via Reuters ‌ ‌ Thanks for reading Newswrap.
